text: Journal of Psychology and Christianity 2007, Vol. 26, No. 4, 307-312 Copyright 2007 Christian Association for P.sychological Studies ISSN 0733-4273 On Creating a Healthy Supervisory Environment: A Christian Relational and Developmental Perspective Richard E. Butman Wheaton College Sandra Johnston Kruse Chicago Area Christian Training Consortium Given the emphasis on building professional competencies, most contemporary supervisory approaches focus largely on the "technical" aspects of becoming a clinician. ^X^^ile this is essential, it is incomplete. This is especially true as Christian supervisors who value a more holistic approach, knowing that our spiri- tual and personal health greatly impacts our professional lives. This article argues for the importance of creating a supervisory environment which, in addition to developing professional competencies, is more holistic in nature and focuses on the character formation of the supervisee as well. The benefits and potential challenges of this approach are discussed. There is a fascinating literature that emerged from the study of traumatized children in the orphanages of Europe in the post World War II era. Their caregivers learned—often through trial and error—that these children needed to hold their bread for the next day if they were going to sleep soundly throughout the night (Linn, Linn, & Linn, 1995). As supervisors at clin- ical training sites, we have often wondered if our supervisees might view us as "transitional objects" as they face the rigors and challenges of actual clinical work. Perhaps the gift of our words and presence serves to provide a "safe holding environment" as they make the often- difficult transition from graduate student to ser- vant-practitioner-scholar. There is no debate in the field about the need to develop essential clinical competencies in future mental health professionals. These are certainly foundational for licensure and effective clinical practice (Frawley-O-Dea & Sarnat, 2001). We are convinced, however, that in order to assist supervisees in developing these compe- tencies, good supervision must be more than an intellectual endeavor. Ideally, it is a highly recip- rocal and collaborative process of mutual search and discovery (Groth-Marnat, 2003). This is not in any way to diminish the importance of "tech- nical competence". But we also believe that exemplary supervision has the potential to deeply imprint the development of character, compassion and convictions as well. At its best, truly impactful supervision can be transforma- Correspondence regarding this article should be addressed to Richard E. Butman, Ph.D., Wheaton Col- lege, Psychology Department, Wheaton, IL 60187; Richard.E.Butman@wheaton.edu tional in terms of the integration of "head, heart and hands" Qones & Butman, 1991). For men and women of faith, this should be viewed as a truly sacred task as it gives us the opportunity to reflect Christ to our supervisees- perhaps akin to offering "bread" to restless supervisees who have yet to learn what truly sustains them in this important work of healing and helping. A Relational and Developmental Approach What does it mean to take a more develop- mental and relational approach to supervision? Initially, this suggests to us that we need to do a careful and thorough assessment of basic inter- personal skills and sensitivities. In addition to establishing a baseline understanding of core clinical competencies (Korchin, 1976), it is per- haps equally important for supervisors to know something about the supervisees' essential life skills. We believe knowledge of their social sup- port systems (e.g., "Who are your friends?"), emerging sense of efficacy (e.g., "What do you do well?"), and overarching sense of meaning and purpose in life (e.g., "What values truly motivate you to do this work?"), are powerful predictors of future effectiveness as mental health professionals (Pargament, 1997). Periodic attention to these matters may ensure better cop- ing strategies, reduce "compassion fatigue", and reduce the professional isolation that all too often leads to serious ethical violations. More- over, as Christian practitioners, we know that paying attention to one's spiritual health and maturity will likely have a positive impact on one's professional life as a result. Effective supervisors also need to pay special attention to the "dance" between supervisor and 307 308 SUPERVISORY ENVIRONMENT supervisee—especially in terms of such key dynamics as anger, intimacy and deception (Lerner, 1985). We have come to appreciate the need to pay attention to the supervisory relation- ship itself, which includes the need to attend to relational repairs as appropriate throughout the course of supervision. In the midst of the stress- ful training year, conflict is inevitable. How it is dealt with—effectively or ineffectively—can speak volumes about the nature of the therapeu- tic alliance (Casement, 2002). We are firmly con- vinced that honest and frank feedback throughout the course of the supervisory rela- tionships is absolutely essential—even beyond that which is "required" by professional bodies (e.g., APA, APPIC). Indeed, such feedback needs to go both ways—if only to deepen the depth and authenticity of a mutually respectful and reciprocal relationship. Effective supervisors need to fully grasp the implications of the learning and motivation research as well. We have increasingly become aware of the power of credible role modeling in the supervisory relationship (Garber, 1995). By any measure, modeling has more impact than direct teaching. In a very real sense, it can be said that what we actually do is far more impor- tant than what we say. At the risk of adding one more maxim to the supervisory literature, how we treat our supervisees and colleagues speaks "volumes" about our integrity and professional identity. We deeply "imprint" our charges—for better or worse. Furthermore, we have come to see the power of disciplined reflection on relevant clinical experiences—(e.g., asking questions such as "What did you see? What did you hear? What does it all mean? How does this all relate to your assumptions about people , problems and change?")—over and against more directive and advice-giving roles. Former interns have consis- tently told us that helping them to learn was more valuable than telling them . Learning to give the type of feedback that is affirming, help- ful, honest and relevant is absolutely essential for professional development (Corey, 2000). We also want our supervisee to be "uncom- monly decent" (Mouw, 1992). In other words, we want them to learn how to more effectively deal with the reality of individual differences in ways that are more "civil" and "convicted". In our current post-modern culture, our profession may run the risk of socializing graduate students to be "accepting", "nice", and highly relativistic. When inevitable differences occur over values, supervisees may shrink from their own values out of a fear of imposing them on others (Sanders, 1997). We want our supervisees to be able to clearly articulate their core beliefs about persons, psychopathology and change. Yet, helping them to have "the courage of their con- victions", while still respecting the values and convictions of others, can be a major profession- al challenge. The deeper risk is that their implicit or covert assumptions are imposed-either inten- tionally or chaotically. Respectful and honest dia- logue does not shrink from differences of opinion on beliefs and/or lifestyle choices (Sande, 2004). Rather than being merely peace- keepers, we want the next generation of servant- practitioner-scholars to be peacemakers, who follow Christ's example to speak the truth in love and humility. With reference to such important charges, we are strongly convinced that good supervisors must be fully cognizant of what values and assumptions they are prompting, shaping and reinforcing in their supervisees in word and deed. We have come to see the importance of "prescriptive psychotherapy" (Harwood, 2005), whereby careful attention is given to matching supervisor and supervisee on relational and interactional variables. Our fear is that these decisions are more often based on assigned roles and responsibilities rather than on our knowl- edge of what "styles" work best with whom. At a minimal level, this means that the supervi- sor needs to know what he or she brings to the supervisory sessions in terms of personality and temperament. In particular, the supervisor needs to fully grasp the risks and benefits of their approaches—not just theoretically—but at a more personal and interpersonal level. Such awareness potentially gives the supervisor a deeper apprecia- tion for when to "speak the truth in love". Poor or ineffectual supervision tends to be "technique-ori- ented" and highly pragmatic-often to the neglect of a deeper understanding of important contextu- al, situational or developmental variables. The evi- dence is clear, however, that keen understanding of contextual and developmental factors promotes lasting change more effectively than problem-solv- ing alone (McMinn & Campbell, 2007). Moving Beyond a Competency-Based Approach (Only) In recent years, there has been a great deal of momentum in the field of psychology to identify BUTMAN AND KRUSE 309 various competencies essential for practicing psy- chologists (APPIC competencies work group, 2002), This work has been immensely helpful to graduate programs and training sites in identifying the requisite skills needed at various stages of training, as well as to practicing psychologists who wish to hone their skills and engage in ongoing "best practice". This is especially relevant as Christian pi-actitioners who, in addition to hav- ing a professional mandate to engage in best practice, also have a spiritual mandate which compels them to emulate Christ by honoring each person through compassionate, excellent care. Despite the clear need for cultivating compe- tencies in current and future clinicians, however, maintaining a focus on competencies alone appears to be short-sighted. Further, this focus on competencies alone may mn the risk of creat- ing a culture of "checklists" which reduces the acquisition of essential core professional compe- tencies to a cookbook (i,e,, "If I learn this list of skills, then I will be competent"). And while growing in the identified professional competen- cies is crucial, a more nuanced, holistic approach to training needs to also include the cultivation of moral virtues or character qualities befitting a psychologist. This shift in emphasis is consistent with others in the field that have argued for greater attention to be paid to the moral character of psycholo- gists, and who have identified character traits such as integrity, prudence, courage and caring as important to practitioners (Johnson & Camp- bell, 2002; Doherty, 1995), We agree that these character traits are vital, but would also argue that having an ethic of justice needs to be added to the list. In fact, an ethic of justice seems par- ticularly central to the heart of God, as seen in Christ's description of those who are blessed by the Father as being those who administer justice to "the least of these" (Matthew 35:34-40), This being said, is it possible to cultivate character traits in trainees? And if so, how? We'd like to propose that it is possible to cultivate these val- ues through a synergistic combination of authen- tic role-modeling, disciplined reflection on both the pragmatics and dynamics of real life clinical applications, and strong—perhaps almost "counter-cultural"—professional communities that are deeply committed to providing truly excellent mental health services, A vexing question in measuring the effective- ness of psychotherapy is deciding what "strate- gies" work best with what combination of client. therapist and contextual factors. Similarly, the common challenge in supervision is matching the style of supervision to fit with the person and needs of the supervisee, Johnson (2007) proposes that various styles of supervision exist on a continuum from a more skill focused, com- petency-based, directive, and structured approach at one end, to a more relational, holis- tic, focus on professional identity at the other. Most supervisors in the field would agree that it is prudent to start a supervisory relationship at a more foundational level, in order to provide suf- ficient structure regarding expectations, organiza- tional policies, and to assist in the development of clinical competencies. However, as a supervisee progresses in his or her training and shows evidence of growing competence in case formulation and clinical skills, their needs in supervision are likely to progress as well. As they develop, in order for supervision to remain relevant and effective it must adapt to the supervisee's changing needs by broadening its scope to include other aspects of the supervisee's development, A Mentorship Model of Supervision Recent literature suggests that students who have been mentored by a trusted faculty mem- ber or supervisor are more likely to thrive both personally and professionally. Some of these benefits include increased career satisfaction and success, a heightened level of professional com- petence, enhanced ability to create and maintain collegial relationships, greater confidence, a more solid professional identity and higher rates of emotional health (e,g,, Johnson, 2007; John- son, 2006; Johnson & Huwe, 2003; Liang, Tracy, Taylor, & Williams, 2002), These findings are compelling and demonstrate clear benefits of mentorship both for the next generation of psy- chologists and, one could argue, for the field at large. Nonetheless, despite these demonstrated benefits, it appears that this style of mentoring supervision is not common (Johnson, 2007; Ponce, Williams & Allen, 2005), It appears, then, that a supervision framework that builds competencies and then moves on to also focus on character formation through men- toring relationships, is greatly needed. Transfor- mational supervision is one model that attempts to bridge this gap. Its distinguishing features are described as ",,, a developmental relationship,,,, [where] supervisors see themselves as deliberate- ly partnering with supervisees to shepherd them 310 SuPERvtsoRY ENVIRONMENT safely through vulnerable transitions ... work[ing] to hone clinical competencies while showing concern for the supervisee's broader welfare and professional development ..." (John- son, 2007, p. 262). In sum, transformational supervision is relational, safe, reciprocal and holistic, focusing on professional as well as per- sonal development. Even so, this expanded role of supervision as more relational and holistic in nature has some important implications. Supervisors must commu- nicate in word and deed a respect for the com- plexities of good psychotherapy, which includes modeling an approach that strikes a good balance between both the art and science of psychothera- py. Eor example, comprehensive training in evi- dence based practice should include the literature on both evidenced based treatments and empiri- cally supported relationships (Norcross, 2002). Supervisees should be taught that the literature strongly suggests that efficacious psychotherapy consists of 15% hope, 15% technique, 30% rela- tional variables, and 40% contextual variables (McMinn & Campbell, 2007). In this way, supervi- sion becomes an invitation to move beyond a sole focus on the technical and scientific aspects of the work to also embrace more of the humane, rela- tional and creative components as well (including a renewed appreciation for the client narrative). Moreover, given the reality that contextual and relationship variables matter, an effective super- visory approach would do well to also incorpo- rate a community psychology perspective, a paradigm that moves beyond the focus on the individual to that of the community/context. This approach's emphasis on strengths, social sup- ports and prevention provides a welcome cor- rective to a deficit-focused, individualistic mindset and fits with a Christian worldview in the way it more fully honors personhood and community in the process. Building Credibility and Mutual Respect Much of what we have said so far clearly implies that supervisors need to be authentic role models that treat supervisees with the utmost respect. An approach to supervision that is perhaps more "formulaic" than foundational runs the risk of developing clinicians that are "compliant" but not necessarily deep. Instead, we need to cultivate clinicians who are able to be deeply engaged and present with matters of the soul, and who do not shrink away from grappling with suffering, sin and injustice. Eirst and foremost, then, supervisors need to be men and women of deep awareness and understand- ing who both model these behaviors and treat their charges accordingly. Eurther, graduate school has a tendency to prompt students to become "field-dependent" (i.e., looking to authority figures to provide the necessary cues on how to think and behave). Perhaps one of the greatest risks of a more "authoritarian" approach to supervision is that it continues this pattern of unhealthy dependency and thwarts the development of true profession- al autonomy. Likewise, a more "permissive" supervisory style tends to encourage a sense of entitlement and unhealthy independence. At a deeper level, it tacitly or even overtly encour- ages a climate of "image management" rather than truth telling and truth seeking. Considering how powerful good supervision can be at this stage of professional identity development, we think that is a tragedy. New clinicians often feel quite vulnerable when they begin to think "outside the box". If the initial role of the supervisor is to encourage appropriate risk-taking, then it is imperative that we also offer a "safe holding environment" as well. Again, that will largely depend on whether or not there is a climate of mutual respect and obvious rapport. Almost by definition, clinical work is a very risky endeavor. Listening to the stories of hurting persons can be overwhelming to the supervisee without a strong sense of self and a healthy social support system. It can be especially stressful for the supervisee to learn how to "prioritize" presenting concerns and decide how best to respond. The reality of psy- chopathology can encourage the development of a mindset of illness often to the exclusion of a more strengths-based, holistic and preventative approach. Good supervision needs to "normal- ize" the doubt and potential disillusionment that comes with the realization of the human condi- tion that can threaten realistic, biblical hope. A more authentic and collaborative relationship helps supervisor and supervisee face these fears together and offer those "soul searching" yet hopeful conversations that can leave a powerful imprint on both for life (Smedes, 2005). We find it especially satisfying when we observe supervisees developing their own clini- cal "voices"—rather than "borrowing" them from others. When challenged to move beyond that which is "safe" and "comfortable", they learn to be both priestly and prophetic in their words BUTMAN AND KRUSE 311 and actions. When this occurs, supervision seems especially empowering, even transforma- tional. Supervisees who are thus empowered seem increasingly willing to address structural and systemic evil—and the consequences of tragic personal choices. Granted, effective super- vision is not about "moralizing," but it certainly needs to address questions about injustice, evil and sin, which is precisely where our Christian framework is in a unique position to speak to these issues. Perhaps more so than more formal academic training, good supervision takes the time to deal with "moral dilemmas" in truly prin- cipled and thoughtful ways, thus helping super- visees to more overtly flesh out their Christian worldview. Frankly, we want to see a great con- gruity of beliefs and behaviors in the next gener- ation of ethical and responsible mental health professionals (Sanders, 1997). Facing the Risks and Responsibilities of this Supervisory Approach Many supervisors may have been socialized to engage in a more traditional, hierarchical approach to supervision, or may choose that approach due to a belief that is "safer" or more "ethical." Certainly, the higher level of congruen- cy and transparency that is required of both supervisor and supervisee in a more relational/transformational approach creates potential risks and responsibilities that need to be addressed and monitored. As in all things, this supervisory approach needs to be employed with wisdom and consideration of the ethical issues involved. Given the greater level of open- ness, trust and collegiality inherent in this super- visory approach, the boundaries between supervisor and supervisee may be characterized by a measure of greater flexibility as compared to a more traditional or hierarchical approach in which boundaries are less fluid. In fact, the authentic nature of the relational/transformation- al supervisory approach requires the boundaries in supervision to be more flexible. It goes without saying, however, that this greater level of flexibility in no way implies a disregard for the clear ethical parameters which strictly prohibit the supervisory relationship from becoming romantic or using the power differen- tial to exploit the supervisee in any way. Instead, we are advocating for a judicious use of flexible, or softer, boundaries that still actively work to protect the supervisee from harm while optimiz- ing his or her growth at the same time. The key in facing the risks and responsibilities of this supervisory approach lies in keeping the protection of the supervisee paramount. One way to do this may be to provide "truth in advertising" about this particular supervisory approach prior to the commencement of super- vision (e.g., during interviews for internship positions) so that supervisees are aware of, and can fully consent to, this more relational style of supervision. Additionally, the supervisor can also initiate a discussion during the initial stages of supervision about incorporating this relational approach, so that supervisees are fully informed and aware of the expectations involved. It is also important for the supervisor to be aware of his or her own countertransference (or emotional reactions) as a supervisor and to seek feedback and/or consultation from colleagues as needed. This honest self-appraisal and the sup- portive accountability of colleagues can facilitate the maintenance of a healthy supervisory envi- ronment on an ongoing basis. In describing the challenging role of the super- visor in transformational supervision, Johnson (2007) aptly writes, "... the supervisor must be comfortably flexible in balancing supportive, coaching and evaluative roles" (p. 262). This description rightly highlights the various supervi- sory roles that are potentially in tension, yet also draws attention to how this can be accomplished through a comfortable level of flexibility, balance and continuous monitoring. Even more than other supervisory approaches, relational/transformational supervision requires attention to roles and expectations. It is not just about being supportive, but about being honest, truthful and evaluative. As one colleague has argued from the context of Latin America (Sierra, 2002), it is more akin to "discipleship" than a more dyadic relationship. It is imperative, then, for the supervisor to be very explicit and overt about his or her objectives beyond the responsi- bility of developing professional competence. Conclusion Biblical wisdom repeatedly highlights how our internal characteristics and/or character qualities largely shape our actions (e.g. Luke 6:45, Matthew 12:34: "out of the heart the mouth speaks" etc.) This reality has clear implications for us as supervisors, and challenges us to create a supervisory environment that honors both the personal and professional aspects of our super- visees. In fact, as Christian practitioners we 312 SUPERVISORY ENVIRONMENT should be more compelled than most to employ this approach to supervision given its holistic focus on the person of the supervisee (personal- ly, spiritually and professionally) and focus on maturation in all spheres of life. In this way, we aspire to "disciple" the next generation of practi- tioners with integrity and intentionality. References APPIC Professional Competencies Workgroups (2002).
